lessons.title: Angles in radians
lessons.summary: Move between degrees, radians and numbers of turns.
lessons.objective: Move between degrees, radians and numbers of turns.
lessons.before: Measure the short curved distance between the radii. If that distance equals the radius, the central angle is one radian.
lessons.ideas:
The fraction of one revolution is \(\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\). A half-turn is \(\pi\text{ rad}=180^\circ\).

Degrees to radians uses \(\frac{\pi}{180}\). Radians to degrees uses \(\frac{180}{\pi}\).

Reduce by \(2\pi\) only when the question asks for direction within one full turn.
lessons.method:
Write the units beside each answer when the question switches between degrees and radians.

Check using 90 degrees. Its radian measure must be half of pi.

Give the total angle and the reduced angle separately if both are requested.
mistakes: Radians measure the central angle. They are not length units.
Swapping the two factors does not cancel the angle's initial unit.
Removing whole turns early gives the wrong total distance travelled.

examples.title: Measuring a turn in two units
examples.question:
A scanner arm of length \(16\) cm rotates about one end through \(72^\circ\).

  1. Convert the rotation to radians.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact length of the arc traced on the rim.

    [2]

  3. Find the angle in radians for the rest of the full circle.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) One half-turn is \(180^\circ=\pi\text{ rad}\). Multiply \(72^\circ\) by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\), then simplify.

\(\frac{2}{5}\pi\) rad.

(b) Use the angle in radians in \(s=r\theta\). The radius is \(16\) cm.

\(\frac{32}{5}\pi\) cm.

(c) A complete turn is \(2\pi\). Subtract the given angle from this total.

\(\frac{8}{5}\pi\) rad.

examples.title: Measuring a turn in two units
examples.question:
A marker on the rim of a disc of radius \(20\) cm turns through \(\frac{11}{12}\pi\) radians.

  1. Give the angle in degrees.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact length of the arc traced on the rim.

    [2]

  3. Find the angle in radians for the rest of the full circle.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Multiply the radian measure by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\). The factor of \(\pi\) cancels.

\(165\) °.

(b) Use the angle in radians in \(s=r\theta\). The radius is \(20\) cm.

\(\frac{55}{3}\pi\) cm.

(c) A complete turn is \(2\pi\). Subtract the given angle from this total.

\(\frac{13}{12}\pi\) rad.

examples.title: Tracking repeated rotations
examples.question:
A control knob of radius \(10\) cm turns through \(45^\circ\) at each of \(4\) identical movements in the same direction.

  1. Find the total angle turned, in radians.

    [2]

  2. Find the total distance moved by a point on the rim.

    [2]

  3. Find the least non-negative angle giving the same final direction, in radians.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The total before any reduction is \(180\) degrees. Convert this by multiplying by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\).

\(\pi\) rad.

(b) The point travels the arc for each movement, including any complete turns.

Multiply the total angle in radians by \(10\).

\(10\pi\) cm.

(c) Each whole turn is \(2\pi\). Remove \(0\) complete turns.

\(\pi\) rad.

lessons.title: Arc lengths and sector perimeters
lessons.summary: Use radian angles to find curves and count the complete boundary.
lessons.objective: Use radian angles to find curves and count the complete boundary.
lessons.before: The larger the turn, the further a point on the rim travels. For a fixed radius, doubling the angle doubles the arc length.
lessons.ideas:
An angle of \(\theta\) radians gives arc length \(s=r\theta\). The result uses the same length unit as the radius.

The perimeter is \(P=2r+r\theta\). If perimeter is given, subtract both radii to find the arc.

With the arc length fixed, \(\theta=s/r\). Both arcs must use the same length unit before their sizes are compared.
lessons.method:
Check a full turn. It gives the familiar circumference \(2\pi r\).

Sketch radii and arc in different colours when the question gives a perimeter.

Check that the angle you find is physically possible for the described part of a circle.
mistakes: An angle in degrees must be converted before using the formula.
The arc formula gives the curved piece only.
An equal arc length does not imply an equal angle.

examples.title: From an arc to the whole sector edge
examples.question:
A curved edge joins the ends of two \(27\) cm radii. The angle at the centre is \(\frac{1}{6}\pi\) radians.

  1. Find the length of the curved edge.

    [2]

  2. Find the length of the remaining arc of the same circle.

    [2]

  3. Find the perimeter of a sector with the original angle and a radius \(16\) cm longer.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Multiply the radius \(27\) by the given radian angle.

\(\frac{9}{2}\pi\) cm.

(b) The remaining sector angle is \(\frac{11}{6}\pi\) radians.

Keep the centre and radius fixed as you use \(s=r\theta\) again.

\(\frac{99}{2}\pi\) cm.

(c) The larger sector has radius \(43\) cm and still subtends the original angle.

Add both new radial sides and its longer arc.

\(86+\frac{43}{6}\pi\) cm.

examples.title: From an arc to the whole sector edge
examples.question:
A complete sector boundary of radius \(31\) cm has perimeter \(62+\frac{31}{2}\pi\) cm.

  1. Find the exact angle at the centre, in radians.

    [2]

  2. Find the length of the remaining arc of the same circle.

    [2]

  3. Find the perimeter of a sector with the original angle and a radius \(19\) cm longer.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The radii contribute \(62\) cm to the perimeter. The arc therefore has length \(\frac{31}{2}\pi\) cm.

Divide the arc length by \(31\).

\(\frac{1}{2}\pi\) rad.

(b) The remaining sector angle is \(\frac{3}{2}\pi\) radians.

Keep the centre and radius fixed as you use \(s=r\theta\) again.

\(\frac{93}{2}\pi\) cm.

(c) The larger sector has radius \(50\) cm and still subtends the original angle.

Add both new radial sides and its longer arc.

\(100+25\pi\) cm.

examples.title: The same arc length on different circles
examples.question:
A sector of radius \(20\) cm has angle \(\frac{3}{2}\pi\) radians. A second circle of radius \(23\) cm has an arc of equal length.

  1. Find the angle subtended by the arc on the second circle.

    [3]

  2. Find the perimeter of the sector associated with the second arc.

    [2]

  3. Explain why the angle is smaller on the second circle.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) The common arc length is \(30\pi\) cm.

Divide it by the second radius, \(23\) cm.

\(\frac{30}{23}\pi\) rad.

(b) The sector edge uses the given arc and the two new radii.

\(46+30\pi\) cm.

(c) With \(s\) fixed, \(\theta=s/r\) decreases as the radius increases.

For a fixed arc length, the angle is inversely proportional to radius.

lessons.title: Sector areas and inverse problems
lessons.summary: Find sector areas and recover missing quantities from an arc or an area.
lessons.objective: Find sector areas and recover missing quantities from an arc or an area.
lessons.before: The whole disc has area πr². A sector occupies the fraction of its turn measured in radians divided by a full turn.
lessons.ideas:
This gives \(A=\frac12r^2\theta\), with the result in square units.

Use \(r=\sqrt{\frac{2A}{\theta}}\) when the angle and area are known.

Using \(s=r\theta\) gives \(A=\frac12rs\). Recover the radius before using the original formulas.
lessons.method:
Check that a half-turn gives half the area of a disc.

Keep all factors of pi until they can cancel algebraically.

One of the two equations should lose its angle when you combine them.
mistakes: The radius is squared even if the answer involves a fraction of pi.
The radius is not twice the area divided by the angle. That gives the radius squared.
The second equation uses the curved arc length, not the sector perimeter.

examples.title: Using arc, area and radius together
examples.question:
A sector has radius \(24\) cm and angle \(\frac{5}{6}\pi\) radians.

  1. Find the exact area of the sector.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact perimeter of the sector.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact area of a sector with the same angle and twice the radius.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) A fraction \(\frac{5}{12}\) of the complete circle is used.

Equivalently, replace the radius and radian angle in \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\).

\(240\pi\) cm².

(b) The arc is \(20\pi\) cm and the two radial sides total \(48\) cm.

\(48+20\pi\) cm.

(c) The angle stays unchanged. Doubling the radius multiplies its square by four.

\(960\pi\) cm².

examples.title: Using arc, area and radius together
examples.question:
A circular sector has area \(\frac{845}{3}\pi\) cm² and angle \(\frac{5}{6}\pi\) radians.

  1. Find the radius of the circle.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact perimeter of the sector.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact area of a sector with the same angle and twice the radius.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Rearrange \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\) to give \(r^2=\frac{2A}{\theta}\).

The factors of pi cancel to give \(r^2=676\). Choose the positive radius.

\(26\) cm.

(b) The arc is \(\frac{65}{3}\pi\) cm and the two radial sides total \(52\) cm.

\(52+\frac{65}{3}\pi\) cm.

(c) The angle stays unchanged. Doubling the radius multiplies its square by four.

\(\frac{3380}{3}\pi\) cm².

examples.title: Using arc, area and radius together
examples.question:
The curved boundary of a sector is \(\frac{58}{15}\pi\) cm long. Its area is \(\frac{841}{15}\pi\) cm².

  1. Find the radius of the sector.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact perimeter of the sector.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact area of a sector with the same angle and twice the radius.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Replace \(r\theta\) by \(s\) in \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\). Then \(r=\frac{2A}{s}\).

Divide twice the area by the given arc length to obtain \(29\) cm.

\(29\) cm.

(b) The arc is \(\frac{58}{15}\pi\) cm and the two radial sides total \(58\) cm.

\(58+\frac{58}{15}\pi\) cm.

(c) The angle stays unchanged. Doubling the radius multiplies its square by four.

\(\frac{3364}{15}\pi\) cm².

lessons.title: Chords and circular segments
lessons.summary: Use triangle geometry to find the straight chord and area between chord and arc.
lessons.objective: Use triangle geometry to find the straight chord and area between chord and arc.
lessons.before: Join the ends of the chord to the centre to make an isosceles triangle. Its angle bisector meets the chord at a right angle.
lessons.ideas:
One half of the chord has length \(r\sin(\theta/2)\). Double this for the whole length.

Subtract the triangle area \(\frac12r^2\sin\theta\) from the sector area \(\frac12r^2\theta\).

The larger segment perimeter uses the major arc and the same chord. Neither radius is on the segment boundary.
lessons.method:
Use the half-angle for the right triangle, and the full angle for the arc.

Quote each area before subtracting. This makes the region you are finding clear.

Check that the major segment area is at least half the disc.
mistakes: The chord is straight. The arc between the same endpoints is longer.
The triangle formula has a sine. The sector formula uses the radian value itself.
Using the minor arc gives the other perimeter.

examples.title: The region cut off by a chord
examples.question:
A chord \(AB\) of a circle of radius \(23\) cm subtends a smaller angle of \(\frac{2}{3}\pi\) radians at the centre \(O\).

  1. Find the exact length of \(AB\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact area of triangle \(AOB\).

    [2]

  3. Find the area of the smaller circular segment, giving your answer exactly.

    [3]
examples.solution:
(a) Bisect the isosceles triangle \(AOB\). Each half has hypotenuse \(23\) and opposite angle \(\frac{1}{3}\pi\).

The whole chord length is \(2r\sin(\theta/2)\).

\(23\sqrt{3}\) cm.

(b) Both enclosing sides of the triangle have length \(23\) cm.

Use \(\frac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta\) with the included angle.

\(\frac{529}{4}\sqrt{3}\) cm².

(c) The smaller sector has area \(\frac{529}{3}\pi\) cm².

The triangle contributes \(\frac{529}{4}\sqrt{3}\) cm². The segment is the sector with that triangle removed.

\(\frac{529}{3}\pi-\frac{529}{4}\sqrt{3}\) cm².

examples.title: The region cut off by a chord
examples.question:
A chord \(AB\) of a circle of radius \(13\) cm subtends a smaller angle of \(\frac{2}{3}\pi\) radians at the centre \(O\).

  1. Find the area of the smaller circular segment, giving your answer exactly.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact length of \(AB\).

    [2]

  3. Find the perimeter of the smaller segment, exactly.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The smaller sector has area \(\frac{169}{3}\pi\) cm².

The triangle contributes \(\frac{169}{4}\sqrt{3}\) cm². The segment is the sector with that triangle removed.

\(\frac{169}{3}\pi-\frac{169}{4}\sqrt{3}\) cm².

(b) Bisect the isosceles triangle \(AOB\). Each half has hypotenuse \(13\) and opposite angle \(\frac{1}{3}\pi\).

The whole chord length is \(2r\sin(\theta/2)\).

\(13\sqrt{3}\) cm.

(c) The arc has length \(\frac{26}{3}\pi\) cm. The straight edge is the chord of length \(13\sqrt{3}\) cm.

\(\frac{26}{3}\pi+13\sqrt{3}\) cm.

examples.title: The region cut off by a chord
examples.question:
A chord \(AB\) of a circle of radius \(17\) cm subtends a smaller angle of \(\frac{1}{3}\pi\) radians at the centre \(O\).

  1. Find the area of the larger circular segment, giving your answer exactly.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact length of \(AB\).

    [2]

  3. Find the perimeter of the larger segment, exactly.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Find the smaller segment by subtracting the triangle area \(\frac{289}{4}\sqrt{3}\) from the smaller sector area \(\frac{289}{6}\pi\).

Subtract the smaller segment area from the full disc.

\(\frac{1445}{6}\pi+\frac{289}{4}\sqrt{3}\) cm².

(b) Bisect the isosceles triangle \(AOB\). Each half has hypotenuse \(17\) and opposite angle \(\frac{1}{6}\pi\).

The whole chord length is \(2r\sin(\theta/2)\).

\(17\) cm.

(c) The arc has length \(\frac{85}{3}\pi\) cm. The straight edge is the chord of length \(17\) cm.

\(\frac{85}{3}\pi+17\) cm.

lessons.title: Compound circular areas and boundaries
lessons.summary: Separate compound shapes into sectors, parts of circles and straight-edged regions.
lessons.objective: Separate compound shapes into sectors, parts of circles and straight-edged regions.
lessons.before: Draw the smaller and larger sectors at the same centre. The region between their arcs is the ring sector.
lessons.ideas:
Subtract to get \(A=\frac12\theta(R^2-r^2)\). Its straight edges each have length \(R-r\).

Use the straight lengths and arcs on the outline for perimeter. Split the interior into non-overlapping shapes for area.

Use the area of the right triangles formed by radii and tangents. Subtract the appropriate sector to isolate the gap.
lessons.method:
Use the sum of arc lengths for perimeter and the difference of sector areas for area.

For a cut-out, record each length removed before adding the new arc.

Mark the right angles and the half-angle before working with trigonometry.
mistakes: The inner arc is still part of the boundary even though its sector area is removed.
A diameter shared by a semicircle and a rectangle does not belong to their combined perimeter.
Applying the tangent ratio to the full central angle uses the wrong triangle.

examples.title: A ring sector with concentric arcs
examples.question:
A ring sector lies between radii \(5\) cm and \(21\) cm, with central angle \(\frac{3}{4}\pi\) radians.

  1. Find the exact area of the ring sector.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact perimeter of the ring sector.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact difference between the lengths of the two arcs.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The sectors have the same angle. Subtract the smaller one, using \(A=\frac{1}{2}\theta(R^2-r^2)\) for their difference.

\(156\pi\) cm².

(b) The outer and inner arcs total \(\frac{39}{2}\pi\) cm.

Each straight edge has length \(16\) cm.

\(32+\frac{39}{2}\pi\) cm.

(c) The shared angle is \(\frac{3}{4}\pi\) radians. The two radii differ by \(16\) cm.

\(12\pi\) cm.

examples.title: Follow the outer boundary
examples.question:
A running track consists of a rectangle of straight length \(10\) m and width \(14\) m, with a semicircle added to each shorter edge.

  1. Find the exact outer perimeter.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact area enclosed.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact increase in area if each straight section is lengthened by 4 m with the same width.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The two straight parts have total length \(20\) m. Together the two semicircles contribute the circumference of a circle of radius \(7\) m.

\(20+14\pi\) m.

(b) The rectangular area is \(140\) m². Combine the two semicircular areas into \(49\pi\) m².

\(140+49\pi\) m².

(c) The two semicircles are unchanged. A rectangular strip 4 m long is added.

\(56\) m².

examples.title: The gap between two tangents and an arc
examples.question:
A circle has centre \(O\) and radius \(14\) cm. The tangents at \(A\) and \(B\) meet at \(T\). The smaller angle \(AOB\) is \(\frac{2}{3}\pi\) radians.

  1. Find the exact length of \(AT\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact area of quadrilateral \(OATB\).

    [2]

  3. Find the exact area bounded by the two tangent segments and the minor arc \(AB\).

    [3]
examples.solution:
(a) The radius meets the tangent at a right angle. The line \(OT\) bisects angle \(AOB\) because the two right triangles have a common hypotenuse and equal radii.

Use \(AT=r\tan(\theta/2)\).

\(14\sqrt{3}\) cm.

(b) Its two congruent right triangles each have area \(\frac12 r\cdot AT\). Add them.

\(196\sqrt{3}\) cm².

(c) The minor sector uses angle \(\frac{2}{3}\pi\) and has area \(\frac{196}{3}\pi\) cm².

Subtract this sector from the full quadrilateral.

\(196\sqrt{3}-\frac{196}{3}\pi\) cm².

lessons.title: Mixed circular measure problems
lessons.summary: Decide which lengths or areas to keep as shapes and constraints change.
lessons.objective: Decide which lengths or areas to keep as shapes and constraints change.
lessons.before: Draw the chord joining the intersections. Each side of that chord contributes one segment to the overlap.
lessons.ideas:
The two segment areas add. Only their curved edges survive on the outside of the lens.

With area fixed, \(\theta_2=\theta_1\left(\frac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^2\).

If total boundary and radii are known, subtract the straight edges and divide the arc sum by the radius sum.
lessons.method:
Find the angle for each original centre, then calculate each segment.

Check the direction of change before simplifying the new angle.

Confirm that the inferred angle is less than a full turn and use it to verify the perimeter.
mistakes: Adding the two sector areas includes two unwanted triangles.
Using a radius ratio without squaring it preserves arc length instead of area.
Use lengths of both arcs in the perimeter of a ring. Count both short links as well.

examples.title: Two equal circles and their shared region
examples.question:
Two circles have equal radius \(33\) cm. Each centre lies on the other circle. The common chord has endpoints \(A\) and \(B\).

  1. Find the angle subtended by the shorter arc AB at either centre.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact perimeter of the region inside both circles.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact area of the region inside both circles.

    [3]
examples.solution:
(a) Join the two centres to \(A\) and to \(B\). This forms an equilateral triangle on each side of the centre line.

Each gives \(\frac{1}{3}\pi\) radians at a centre. Add the two angles.

\(\frac{2}{3}\pi\) rad.

(b) Each boundary arc has length \(22\pi\) cm. The complete outline has two such arcs.

\(44\pi\) cm.

(c) Each half of the lens is a minor segment with sector area \(363\pi\) cm².

The triangle for each segment contributes \(\frac{1089}{4}\sqrt{3}\) cm².

Subtract one triangle from each sector and add the two identical segments.

\(726\pi-\frac{1089}{2}\sqrt{3}\) cm².

examples.title: Change the radius and keep the area fixed
examples.question:
The perimeter of a sector with radius \(20\) cm is \(40+5\pi\) cm. A second sector has the same area but radius \(25\) cm.

  1. Find the exact central angle of the first sector.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact area of either sector.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact angle of the second sector.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The curved edge has length \(5\pi\) cm after removing both radial sides.

Divide this arc length by the original radius \(20\) cm.

\(\frac{1}{4}\pi\) rad.

(b) Use the angle and radius of the original sector. The area is preserved by the change.

\(50\pi\) cm².

(c) The second squared radius is \(\frac{25}{16}\) times the first.

To keep \(r^2\theta\) fixed, multiply the first angle by \(\frac{16}{25}\).

\(\frac{4}{25}\pi\) rad.

examples.title: A ring sector with concentric arcs
examples.question:
A ring sector has inner radius \(21\) cm and outer radius \(28\) cm. Its total perimeter is \(14+\frac{147}{5}\pi\) cm.

  1. Find its angle at the common centre.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact area of the ring sector.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact difference between the lengths of the two arcs.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Subtract the two connecting edges, totalling \(14\) cm. The arc sum is \(\frac{147}{5}\pi\) cm.

Divide the arc sum by the sum of the radii \(49\) cm.

\(\frac{3}{5}\pi\) rad.

(b) Use the difference of the two sector areas with angle \(\frac{3}{5}\pi\) radians.

\(\frac{1029}{10}\pi\) cm².

(c) The shared angle is \(\frac{3}{5}\pi\) radians. The two radii differ by \(7\) cm.

\(\frac{21}{5}\pi\) cm.

Convert the rotation to radians.
questions.solution_html:

\(\frac{11}{12}\pi\) rad.

questions.hint_html: Add the turns before converting the total to radians.

Give the angle in degrees.

Multiply the radian measure by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\). The factor of \(\pi\) cancels.

questions.prompt_html:
A scanner arm of length \(14\) cm rotates about one end through \(210^\circ\).

  1. Convert the rotation to radians.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact length of the arc traced on the rim.

    [2]

  3. Find the angle in radians for the rest of the full circle.

A chord \(AB\) of a circle of radius \(30\) cm subtends a smaller angle of \(\frac{1}{2}\pi\) radians at the centre \(O\).

Find the exact length of \(AB\).
questions.solution_html:
Bisect the isosceles triangle \(AOB\). Each half has hypotenuse \(30\) and opposite angle \(\frac{1}{4}\pi\).

The whole chord length is \(2r\sin(\theta/2)\).

\(30\sqrt{2}\) cm.
questions.hint_html: Find half the chord in the right triangle, then double it.

questions.title: The region cut off by a chord
questions.prompt_html:
A chord \(AB\) of a circle of radius \(35\) cm subtends a smaller angle of \(\frac{2}{3}\pi\) radians at the centre \(O\).

Find the area of the smaller circular segment, giving your answer exactly.
questions.solution_html:
The smaller sector has area \(\frac{1225}{3}\pi\) cm².

The triangle contributes \(\frac{1225}{4}\sqrt{3}\) cm². The segment is the sector with that triangle removed.

\(\frac{1225}{3}\pi-\frac{1225}{4}\sqrt{3}\) cm².

\(576\sqrt{3}-192\pi\) cm².

A ring sector has width \(7\) cm, central angle \(\frac{3}{4}\pi\) radians and area \(\frac{1239}{8}\pi\) cm². Its two arcs have the same centre.

  1. Find the inner radius.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact perimeter of the ring sector.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact difference between the lengths of the two arcs.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Write the outer radius as \(r+7\). The difference of the squared radii is \(7(2r+7)\).

Divide the given area by half the central angle to get \(413\). Solve the resulting linear equation.

\(26\) cm.

(b) The outer and inner arcs total \(\frac{177}{4}\pi\) cm.

Each straight edge has length \(7\) cm.

\(14+\frac{177}{4}\pi\) cm.

(c) The shared angle is \(\frac{3}{4}\pi\) radians. The two radii differ by \(7\) cm.

\(\frac{21}{4}\pi\) cm.
questions.hint_html: Use the difference of the sector areas, with both radii expressed using the same unknown.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the difference of the sector areas, with both radii expressed using the same unknown.
Factor the difference of the squares to obtain a linear equation in r.
Add two arcs and two straight edges.
Multiply the common angle by the radial difference.

questions.title: The gap between two tangents and an arc
questions.prompt_html:
A circle has centre \(O\) and radius \(32\) cm. The tangents at \(A\) and \(B\) meet at \(T\). The smaller angle \(AOB\) is \(\frac{1}{2}\pi\) radians.

  1. Find the exact length of \(AT\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact area of quadrilateral \(OATB\).

    [2]

  3. Find the exact area bounded by the two tangent segments and the minor arc \(AB\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a) The radius meets the tangent at a right angle. The line \(OT\) bisects angle \(AOB\) because the two right triangles have a common hypotenuse and equal radii.

Use \(AT=r\tan(\theta/2)\).

\(32\) cm.

(b) Its two congruent right triangles each have area \(\frac12 r\cdot AT\). Add them.

\(1024\) cm².

(c) The minor sector uses angle \(\frac{1}{2}\pi\) and has area \(256\pi\) cm².

Subtract this sector from the full quadrilateral.

\(1024-256\pi\) cm².
questions.hint_html: Use the half-angle in the right triangle.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the half-angle in the right triangle.
Identify which side is opposite the half-angle.
Subtract the minor sector from the kite formed by radii and tangents.
Use the minor angle in the sector area formula.

Two circles have equal radius \(30\) cm. Each centre lies on the other circle. The common chord has endpoints \(A\) and \(B\).

Find the angle subtended by the shorter arc AB at either centre.
questions.solution_html:
Join the two centres to \(A\) and to \(B\). This forms an equilateral triangle on each side of the centre line.

Each gives \(\frac{1}{3}\pi\) radians at a centre. Add the two angles.

\(\frac{2}{3}\pi\) rad.

questions.title: The gap between two tangents and an arc
questions.prompt_html:
A circle has centre \(O\) and radius \(33\) cm. The tangents at \(A\) and \(B\) meet at \(T\). The smaller angle \(AOB\) is \(\frac{1}{3}\pi\) radians.

  1. Find the exact length of \(AT\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact area of quadrilateral \(OATB\).

    [2]

  3. Find the exact area bounded by the two tangent segments and the minor arc \(AB\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a) The radius meets the tangent at a right angle. The line \(OT\) bisects angle \(AOB\) because the two right triangles have a common hypotenuse and equal radii.

Use \(AT=r\tan(\theta/2)\).

\(11\sqrt{3}\) cm.

(b) Its two congruent right triangles each have area \(\frac12 r\cdot AT\). Add them.

\(363\sqrt{3}\) cm².

(c) The minor sector uses angle \(\frac{1}{3}\pi\) and has area \(\frac{363}{2}\pi\) cm².

Subtract this sector from the full quadrilateral.

\(363\sqrt{3}-\frac{363}{2}\pi\) cm².
questions.hint_html: Use the half-angle in the right triangle.
